nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What do the PHH suggest about developing nations with loose environmental regulations?
nodes.answer: The PHH suggest that developing nations with loose environmental regulations become hubs for pollution-intensive production, attracting multinational firms to transfer their highly polluting industries to these areas due to lower manufacturing costs.
nodes.paragraph: The PHH posit that developing nations with loose environmental regulations become hubs for pollution-intensive production, attracting multinational firms to transfer their highly polluting industries to these areas. Manufacturing costs are substantially lower in nations with laxer environmental restrictions, thereby accommodating companies with more detrimental environmental consequences15. Effective environmental regulations, technological transfers, and knowledge spillovers can mitigate carbon-intensive trade activities37. On the other hand, the FEH suggests that a nation S trade patterns are influenced by its resource endowments, leading to the specialisation and export of goods that capitalise on abundant local resources. Developing countries like Somalia, where natural resources are abundant, tend to specialise in resource-intensive manufacturing. This specialisation and increased trade can accelerate environmental degradation due to the higher resource consumption and potential pollution associated with these industries. With the global imperative to combat climate change, the intersection of trade openness, economic growth, environmental sustainability, and globalisation has garnered increasing attention in contemporary literature. Among the top emitters of emerging economies, Ertugrul et al.38 reveal that the vital long-run determinants of environmental degradation are economic growth, energy use, and trade openness.

nodes.question: What percentage of Canadian industries’ expenditures on pollution management was attributed to end-of-pipe abatement in 2021?
nodes.answer: The share of Canadian industries’ expenditure on pollution abatement and control attributed to end-of-pipe abatement was 46.1% in 2021.
nodes.paragraph: Under cross-border profit shifting due to foreign ownership of environ- mental firms, non-cooperative governments have an incentive to weaken their environmental policies to prevent profit outflows. When environmental firms engage in imperfect competition, environmental poli- cies are used to increase the use of environmental goods. Furthermore, Sugiyama et al. (2023) consider the effect of environmental policies on the number of environmental firms. 7 See Greaker and Rosendahl (2008) and Sugiyama et al. (2023). An exception is David and Sinclair- Desgagn (2010) in which the simultaneous choice of taxes and subsidies is considered in a closed econ- omy setting. In a different context than that of this paper, Wan et al. (2018) examine the simultaneous choice of emission taxes and import tariffs when consumption of final goods reduces local pollution. 8 Following David and Sinclair-Desgagn (2010), this paper considers the case of end-of-pipe abate- ment. This abatement activity is an important category of environmental protection. For example, the share of Canadian industries expenditure on pollution abatement and control, which corresponds to end-of-pipe abatement, in air pollution management was 46.1% in 2021; see Capital and Operat- ing Expenditures on Pollution Prevention and Pollution Abatement and Control by Industry (Statistics Canada 2024).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Green manufacturing|Pollution control_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are some of the environmental benefits of implementing environmental protection technologies in the textile industry supply chain?
nodes.answer: By implementing environmental protection technologies, the textile industry can reduce GHG emissions, waste disposal, and wastewater discharge into rivers, creating a cleaner and healthier environment for society.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Green manufacturing|Pollution control_qna_003
nodes.label: Science and Tech
nodes.question: How can air pollution be linked to textile dyeing processes?
nodes.answer: Common textile dyeing processes often involve the use of harmful chemicals and dyes that can release pollutants into the air, contributing to air pollution.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Green manufacturing|Pollution control_qna_004
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What legislative process did the EU begin in 2020 that relates to pollution prevention?
nodes.answer: The EU started a process of revising its Industrial Emissions Directive (IED, 2010/75/EU) in 2020 to endorse the prevention first principle.
nodes.paragraph: Together with the ourishing academic literature on EU-ETS design in recent years (see V erbruggen et al. 2019 , for a review), it has been noticed that the goal of carbon trading is to reduce emissions, not to avoid them. The EU-ETSmandates that industrial plants need to surrender emission allowances corresponding to the amount of GHG they emit, but as long as rms can afford to pay for the extra allowances, they do not need to mitigate their climate impact. This runs against theprevention rst principle stated in the Hierarchy of action on pollution developed by the European Commission, which should be implemented by design and during production (see Plan 2021 ). Coincidentally, the EU in 2020 has started a process of revising its Industrial Emissions Directive (IED, 2010/75/EU), a piece of legislation that fully endorses theprevention rst principle, resulting in a revision proposal published in April 2022 (COM/2022/156 nal/3). Under the IED, pollution prevention is achieved by setting emissions limits for all pollutants before installations are able to operate, as well as other requirements such as energy ef ciency.
